title: the oldest labor law
hook: the oldest labor law; a day the world can't have
tomorrow: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Shema. Six words, eyes covered, that begin with hear. Did you listen to someone all the way to the end of a sentence? Day three.

A phone on a Saturday looks like a phone on a Tuesday. Work email. The group chat. A sale that ends tonight. The world never really closes anymore. Now take a family that, every week, from Friday sunset until the stars come out on Saturday, lets none of that in. No office. No shopping. In some homes, not even a light switch. Not a holiday, not a sick day. Just the seventh day, arriving on schedule. Some people call it the oldest labor law there is: one day in seven when nobody in the house works. Today: the day the world can't have.
screen: `THE WORLD NEVER CLOSES.` → `A DAY IT CAN'T REACH.` → `THE SEVENTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root, shin, bet, tav, that means to stop. To cease. Not first to relax, or to worship, but to stop. The root is already there at the end of the creation story. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "and He rested on the seventh day from all His work which He had made." The Hebrew verb there comes from the same root. In the story, even God stops. English borrowed the word as Sabbath. The day runs from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday, when three stars are out, because in the Torah's story a day starts in the evening. Then the rabbis asked a practical question: what counts as work? The Mishnah lists thirty-nine kinds: planting, baking, writing, building, lighting a fire, and more. The Talmud ties the list to the building of the tabernacle, the tent for God in the desert: the kinds of work it took to make that are the kinds that stop. So work, on Shabbat, means making and changing things, not how tired you get. And the rest isn't only for whoever runs the house. The commandment rests the whole household, a weekly day off written into an ancient law; at the end of this week we'll look at who's on that list. Jews keep the day in different ways. Orthodox Jews keep the thirty-nine categories carefully: no driving, no cooking, no phones. Conservative, Reform and other Jews keep Shabbat in their own ways, through the candles, the meal, synagogue and a slower day, with each community drawing its own lines. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described Shabbat as a palace built in time rather than in space. You don't travel to it. It arrives, every week, wherever you are.
screen: `SHABBAT — TO STOP.` · `ON THE SEVENTH DAY, GOD STOPPED.` · `THIRTY-NINE KINDS OF WORK.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · then, large: `FRIDAY SUNSET TO SATURDAY STARS.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On each breath, put one thing down. First breath: set down the thing you're working on. Second breath: set down the thing you're worried about. Third breath: set down the phone, if it's in your hand. For three breaths, nothing is being made or fixed. That's the whole idea of Shabbat, very small.
Shabbat. To stop. The seventh day, sunset Friday to stars on Saturday, a rest for everyone in the house. Third word.
Your line: stop. it's already Friday. Whatever day it actually is, pick one small stretch today, ten minutes, and treat it like the week is over. Nothing to finish. Day three.

screen: `DAY 3 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWO FLAMES, EIGHTEEN MINUTES BEFORE SUNSET.`

howItsDone: Jews mark Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall with candles, blessings over wine and bread, a family meal and synagogue; observant Jews refrain from the thirty-nine categories of work, while others keep it through the meal, rest and a slower day.

fork.setup: you're a rabbi, and people ask: what exactly counts as work on Shabbat? where do you look for the answer?
options: the building of the tabernacle in the desert.
fork.reveal: the rabbis drew thirty-nine kinds of creative work from the building of the tabernacle. work, on Shabbat, means making, not effort.

original.note: Hebrew: from the root sh-b-t, to stop or cease. English Sabbath comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Jewish day of worship.
what it means: a day of stopping, from Friday sunset to Saturday stars, for everyone in the house, down to the animals.
what a scholar hears: the root sh-b-t means to cease, and Genesis 2:2 uses it for God's own stopping. the Mishnah counts thirty-nine kinds of work; the Talmud ties them to the tabernacle.

Hook rewritten (was 'Think about... Now picture'); cut unsourced 'twenty-five hours', 'three thousand years' and 'may be the oldest rule anywhere'. The tabernacle link is now credited to the Talmud (Shabbat 49b), not the Mishnah. 'Each deciding how much to set down' replaced so Conservative practice isn't framed as individual choice. Confirm the JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 2:2.
'The oldest labor law' (the index title) is now attributed: 'some people call it'; confirm the framing is acceptable.
Thirty-nine categories linked to the tabernacle (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2; Talmud Shabbat 49b): confirm.
Description of observance across movements (Orthodox, Conservative, Reform) is brief and general; confirm it's fair to each.
